newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish premier says not planning early elections.
newsitem.headline: Danish premier says not planning early elections.

text.p: Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen said on Tuesday that he did not intend to exploit turmoil in the opposition Conservative Party by advancing a general election scheduled by September 1998.

He told reporters at his regular weekly news briefing that his minority Social Democrat-led government had a packed legislative programme which took precedence over exploiting other parties' misfortunes.
"The government has much work to do, especially regarding transport, law and order and economic policy. Therefore an election is not something that I am thinking about," he said.

Conservative leader Hans Engell was replaced by his party on Monday after admitting that his blood-alcohol level was well above the legal limit when he drove his car into a lamp post on the way home from a late-night supper meeting.

A Gallup Poll published in the Berlingske Tidende daily on Tuesday showed that the Social Democrats had won support at the Conservatives' expense but that a Conservative-Liberal alliance would still be the biggest bloc if an election were held now.
The poll showed the Social Democrats winning 57 seats, up from 50 in a December survey but down from the 62 they now hold in the 179-seat parliament.
The Conservatives were seen taking 23 seats if a poll were held now, compared to their present 27, and the main opposition Liberals were forecast as winning 51 seats, well up from their current 42.
The Conservatives put on a strong show of unity in radio and television interviews presenting new party chairman Per Stig Moeller and political spokeswoman Karen Hoejte Jensen.

Social Democrat insiders say there are divisions between those who support prime minister Rasmussen's centrist line and attempts to cut government spending and those who say that he has abandoned traditional party values of social compassion and an elaborate welfare state.

Animosity between the premier and the Radical Liberal Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen is an open secret and another coalition partner, the Centre Democrats resigned from the government just before Christmas, saying that it had become too dependent on the far-left parliamentary fringe.

They have pledged to continue voting with the government for the life of the present parliament but could be a wild card in the post-election coalition-building usual in Denmark, where no single party has won an outright majority this century.
